claims.text: A machine-learning approach trained on experimental data and incorporating defect-sensitive features will improve thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy for bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The predicted improvement applies in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The machine-learning approach will be particularly advantageous for HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Existing analytical thermal-conductivity models assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
The target initial state is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model will be trained on experimental thermal-conductivity data that include specimens with known defect concentrations and compositions.
Oxygen concentration, atomic-scale disorder, and local lattice distortions can serve as defect-sensitive predictive features.
Defects and disorder influence phonon scattering and thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
A machine-learning model using defect-sensitive features can capture these defect and disorder effects.
Analytical models based on perfect crystals do not adequately represent defect- and disorder-mediated thermal transport.
The machine-learning approach will reduce thermal-conductivity prediction error by at least 20% relative to the analytical-model baseline.
The approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen concentrations up to 1 wt.%.
The approach is limited to the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature intervals.
Prediction improvement depends on training-data quality and quantity and on the selected machine-learning model.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% error reduction relative to analytical models in either temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.
